content: Suma root, also known as Brazilian ginseng (Pfaffia paniculata and its synonyms such as Hebanthe paniculata, Gomphrena paniculata, and others), is derived from a sprawling ground vine native to South America. Traditionally, it has been utilized as both a medicinal remedy and a tonic. It is colloquially referred to as para todo, meaning for all, due to its wide-ranging therapeutic applications. Suma is classified as an adaptogen, which means it helps to normalize and enhance bodily systems, improve resistance to stress, and promote overall physiological functioning. It has been employed effectively for various ailments, which justifies its nickname. Pharmacologically, suma is believed to support hormonal balance, reduce inflammation, inhibit the growth of cancer and leukemia cells, enhance immune function, and increase libido. It also provides a range of normalizing and rejuvenating effects. One proposed mechanism for its diverse effects is its ability to improve oxygenation and energy efficiency at the cellular level. Suma contains several bioactive compounds, including germanium, beta-ecdysterone, allantoin, and a unique group of phytochemical saponins known as pfaffosides. Historically, the use of related species such as Iresine celosia (also known as Tlantcuayin) dates back approximately 2,000 years to the Maya-Quiché civilization. This plant was documented in the 1552 manuscript Libellus de Medicinalibus Indorum Herbis, which details pre-Columbian medicinal practices. In modern times, during the 1960s to 1980s, Efraín Contreras, a renowned naturopath, identified the anti-tumoral properties of Iresine celosia, a plant native to Central America. During the 1970s and 1980s, Contreras received approval to administer Iresine celosia in both liquid and dry herbal extract forms to patients at hospitals in Managua, Nicaragua. In 1983, the Scientific Commission of the Ministry of Health of Nicaragua evaluated the use of Iresine celosia (referred to as Codin VII) in patients with digestive system tumors, both preand post-surgery. These patients, who had various carcinomas of the stomach and regional lymph nodes, experienced significant tumor size reduction following post-surgical treatment. In cases of mammary gland carcinomas with metastases, local metastases disappeared within 12 to 15 days of treatment, and distant metastases were also reduced. Across all cases where Codin VII was used, patients showed marked improvements in health, including enhanced general well-being, cessation of hemorrhages, vaginal discharges, and pain. Importantly, no toxicity or side effects were observed. In the 1990s, Iresine celosia was administered to patients with prostate issues and sexual impotence, yielding promising results. Research contributions from the Department of Chemistry at Wayne State University in the United States further explored the structure of its active compounds, such as the isoflavone Tlatlancuayin. Iresine celosia was introduced to Europe approximately 15 years ago, and from 1994 to 1998, it was presented at various forums in France, including Cannes, Sophia Antipolis, Biarritz, Lyon, and Paris. Traditional records indicate that Iresine celosia has been used to treat tumoral pathologies affecting the prostate, mammary glands, ovaries, brain, intestines, and more. It has also been employed to enhance libido, address psychiatric conditions, and combat immune system suppression. The plant contains 50% natural glucid steroids, which may contribute to its therapeutic effects. Clinical studies conducted in Nicaragua have demonstrated that Iresine celosia alters the permeability of pathological cells and modifies the bioelectric potential of cancerous cell membranes, as reported by researchers such as Dindail et al.
